items.stem: Let T be a complete and sufficient statistic for a family 𝒫 of distributions and let U be a sufficient statistic for 𝒫. If P_f(T ≥ 0) = 1 for all f ∈ 𝒫, then which one of the following options is NOT necessarily correct?
options: T² is a complete statistic for 𝒫
T² is a minimal sufficient statistic for 𝒫
T is a function of U
U is a function of T
items.explanation: A complete sufficient statistic is minimal sufficient, and a minimal sufficient statistic is a function of every sufficient statistic, so T is a function of U. Because T ≥ 0, T² is a one-to-one function of T, so T² is also complete and minimal sufficient. But a sufficient U can carry more than T (the whole sample, for instance), so U need not be a function of T.

items.stem: Let X₁, X₂ be a random sample from N(θ, 1) distribution, where θ ∈ ℝ. Consider testing H₀: θ = 0 against H₁: θ ≠ 0. Let φ(X₁, X₂) be the likelihood ratio test of size 0.05 for testing H₀ against H₁. Then which one of the following options is correct?
options: φ(X₁, X₂) is a uniformly most powerful test of size 0.05
E_θ(φ(X₁, X₂)) ≥ 0.05 ∀ θ ∈ ℝ
There exists a uniformly most powerful test of size 0.05
E_θ=0(X₁ φ(X₁, X₂)) = 0.05
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio test rejects when √2·|X̄| > 1.96. Its power 1 − Φ(1.96 − √2θ) + Φ(−1.96 − √2θ) is smallest at θ = 0, where it equals 0.05, so the test is unbiased: power ≥ 0.05 everywhere. For a two-sided alternative no UMP test exists, because the one-sided most powerful tests differ for θ > 0 and θ < 0. Under θ = 0 the test is unchanged by (X₁, X₂) → (−X₁, −X₂), so E(X₁φ) = 0, not 0.05.

items.stem: Let a random variable X follow a distribution with density f ∈ {f₀, f₁}, where f₀(x) = 1 if 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and 0 otherwise, and f₁(x) = 1 if 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 and 0 otherwise. Let φ be a most powerful test of level 0.05 for testing H₀: f = f₀ against H₁: f = f₁ based on X. Then which one of the following options is necessarily correct?
options: E_f₁(φ(X)) = 1
items.explanation: The two supports overlap only at the single point 1. The test that rejects when X > 1 has size 0 and power 1, so every most powerful test of level 0.05 must have power 1. It need not use its whole level: it may also reject on any part of [0, 1] of probability up to 0.05, or on none of it, so its size can be anything in [0, 0.05] and P_f₀(φ = 1) need not equal P_f₀(X > 1) = 0.

items.stem: Let X be a random variable having probability density function f ∈ {f₀, f₁}. Let φ be a most powerful test of level 0.05 for testing H₀: f = f₀ against H₁: f = f₁ based on X. Then which one of the following options is NOT necessarily correct?
options: φ is the unique most powerful test of level 0.05
For some constant c ≥ 0, P_f(f₁(X) > cf₀(X)) ≤ P_f(φ(X) = 1), ∀ f ∈ {f₀, f₁}
items.explanation: Level 0.05 means E_f₀(φ) ≤ 0.05. A most powerful test is at least as powerful as the trivial test φ ≡ 0.05, so its power is at least 0.05. By the necessity part of the Neyman–Pearson lemma, a most powerful test rejects (almost surely) wherever f₁ > cf₀ for some c, which gives the last inequality. Uniqueness can fail: on the set where f₁ = cf₀ the test may randomise in many ways, or where both densities vanish it may do anything.

items.stem: Let x₁ = 0, x₂ = 1, x₃ = 1, x₄ = 1 and x₅ = 0 be observed values of a random sample of size 5 from Bin(1, θ) distribution, where θ ∈ (0, 0.7]. Then the maximum likelihood estimate of θ based on the above sample is ________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
items.explanation: The likelihood θ³(1 − θ)² is maximised over (0, 1) at the sample proportion x̄ = 3/5 = 0.6. That value lies inside the allowed range (0, 0.7], so the restriction does not bind and the MLE is 0.60.
items.check: Had x̄ exceeded 0.7, the MLE would have been the boundary value 0.7; compare x̄ with the bound first.

items.stem: Let X₁, …, X₅ be a random sample from N(θ, 6), where θ ∈ ℝ, and let c(θ) be the Cramer-Rao lower bound for the variances of unbiased estimators of θ based on the above sample. Then 15 inf_{θ∈ℝ} c(θ) equals ________ (answer in integer).
items.explanation: For N(θ, σ²) with σ² known, the Fisher information in one observation is 1/σ², so the bound for n observations is σ²/n = 6/5, the same for every θ. Hence 15 × 6/5 = 18.
items.check: X̄ is unbiased with variance σ²/n = 6/5 and attains the bound, so the bound cannot be larger than Var(X̄).

items.stem: Let X₁, …, Xₙ, n ≥ 2, be a random sample from a N(−θ, θ) distribution, where θ > 0 is an unknown parameter. Then which one of the following options is correct?
options: Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ Xᵢ is a minimal sufficient statistic
Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ Xᵢ² is a minimal sufficient statistic
((1/n)ΣXᵢ, (1/(n − 1))Σⱼ(Xⱼ − (1/n)ΣXᵢ)²) is a complete statistic
−(1/n)ΣXᵢ is a uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of θ
items.explanation: The log density is −(x + θ)²/(2θ) − (1/2) ln(2πθ) = −x²/(2θ) − x − θ/2 − (1/2) ln(2πθ). The term −x does not involve θ, so the likelihood depends on the data only through Σxᵢ², which is minimal sufficient (and complete: a one-parameter exponential family). (X̄, S²) is not complete, since E(X̄ + S²) = −θ + θ = 0 for all θ. −X̄ is unbiased but is not a function of ΣXᵢ², so it is not the UMVUE.

items.stem: Let X₁, X₂ be a random sample from a distribution having probability density function f_θ(x) = (1/θ)e^(−x/θ) if x > 0 and 0 otherwise, where θ ∈ (0, ∞) is an unknown parameter. For testing H₀: θ ≤ 1 against H₁: θ > 1, consider the test φ(X₁, X₂) = 1 if X₁ > 1, 0 otherwise. Then which one of the following tests has the same power function as φ?
options: φ₁ = (X₁ + X₂ − 1)/(X₁ + X₂) if X₁ + X₂ > 1, 0 otherwise
φ₂ = (2X₁ + 2X₂ − 1)/(2(X₁ + X₂)) if X₁ + X₂ > 1, 0 otherwise
φ₃ = (3X₁ + 3X₂ − 1)/(3(X₁ + X₂)) if X₁ + X₂ > 1, 0 otherwise
φ₄ = (4X₁ + 4X₂ − 1)/(4(X₁ + X₂)) if X₁ + X₂ > 1, 0 otherwise
items.explanation: Condition φ on the sufficient statistic S = X₁ + X₂ (Rao–Blackwell): given S = s, X₁ is Uniform(0, s), so E(φ | S = s) = P(X₁ > 1 | S = s) = (s − 1)/s for s > 1 and 0 otherwise. A test and its conditional expectation given S have the same expectation under every θ, hence the same power function. The other three equal 1 − 1/(ks) with k > 1, which is larger.

items.stem: Let X₁, …, Xₙ be a random sample from a uniform distribution over the interval (−θ/2, θ/2), where θ > 0 is an unknown parameter. Then which of the following options is/are correct?
statements: 2 max{X₁, …, Xₙ} is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ
(min{X₁, …, Xₙ}, max{X₁, …, Xₙ}) is a sufficient statistic
(min{X₁, …, Xₙ}, max{X₁, …, Xₙ}) is a complete statistic
(2(n + 1)/n) max{|X₁|, …, |Xₙ|} is a uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of θ
options: D only
B only
A, B and D only
B and D only
items.explanation: The whole problem turns on T = max|Xᵢ|: it is the minimal sufficient statistic and it is complete, while the pair (min, max) is sufficient but carries a symmetric ancillary piece that destroys completeness.

A.why: False: the likelihood θ⁻ⁿ needs θ ≥ 2 max|Xᵢ|, so the MLE is 2 max|Xᵢ|; 2 max Xᵢ can even be negative.

B.why: True: the likelihood depends on the data through max|Xᵢ| = max(−min Xᵢ, max Xᵢ), a function of (min, max).

C.why: False: E(min Xᵢ + max Xᵢ) = 0 for every θ by symmetry, though min + max is not zero, so the pair is not complete.

D.why: True: T = max|Xᵢ| is complete sufficient; |Xᵢ| ~ Uniform(0, θ/2) gives E(T) = nθ/(2(n + 1)), so (2(n + 1)/n)T is unbiased and, by Lehmann–Scheffé, the UMVUE.

items.stem: Let X₁, X₂, …, X₇ be a random sample from a population having the probability density function f(x) = (1/2)λ³x²e^(−λx), x > 0, where λ > 0 is an unknown parameter. Let λ̂ be the maximum likelihood estimator of λ, and E(λ̂ − λ) = αλ be the corresponding bias, where α is a real constant. Then the value of 1/α equals ________ (answer in integer).
items.explanation: Each Xᵢ is Gamma(3, λ). The log-likelihood 21 ln λ − λΣxᵢ + const is maximised at λ̂ = 21/S with S = ΣXᵢ ~ Gamma(21, λ). E(1/S) = λ/20, so E(λ̂) = 21λ/20 and the bias is λ/20: α = 1/20 and 1/α = 20.
items.check: For S ~ Gamma(k, λ), E(1/S) = λ/(k − 1), so the MLE kλ/(k − 1) overshoots by a factor k/(k − 1) = 21/20.

items.stem: Let X₁, X₂ be a random sample from a population having probability density function f_θ(x) = e^(x − θ) if −∞ < x ≤ θ, and 0 otherwise, where θ ∈ ℝ is an unknown parameter. Consider testing H₀: θ ≥ 0 against H₁: θ < 0 at level α = 0.09. Let β(θ) denote the power function of a uniformly most powerful test. Then β(logₑ 0.36) equals ________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
items.explanation: The maximum M = max(X₁, X₂) is sufficient, with Pr_θ(M ≤ c) = e^(2(c − θ)) for c ≤ θ. Small values of M point to small θ, so the UMP test rejects when M ≤ c, with size e^(2c) = 0.09 at θ = 0, i.e. c = ln 0.3. At θ = ln 0.36 (> c): β = e^(2c)/e^(2θ) = 0.09/0.36² = 0.09/0.1296 = 0.694, which rounds to 0.69.
items.check: e^(2θ) at θ = ln 0.36 is 0.36² = 0.1296, not 0.36; dividing by 0.36 instead gives the wrong 0.25.

items.stem: Let X ~ Bin(3, θ), where θ ∈ (0, 1) is an unknown parameter. For testing H₀: 1/4 ≤ θ ≤ 3/4 against H₁: θ < 1/4 or θ > 3/4, consider the test φ(x) = 1 if x ∈ {0, 3} and 0 if x ∈ {1, 2}. The size of the test φ is ________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
items.explanation: The rejection probability is θ³ + (1 − θ)³ = 1 − 3θ + 3θ², a parabola with its minimum at θ = 1/2. Over the null interval [1/4, 3/4] its largest value is at the endpoints: (1/4)³ + (3/4)³ = 1/64 + 27/64 = 28/64 = 0.4375, so the size is 0.44.
items.check: Size is the supremum over the whole null set, not the value at its centre (which would be 0.25).
